title: AI Could Help Close the Women's Health Gap, but Better Data Must Come First
excerpt: Women's health captures only 6% of private healthcare investment. Experts say artificial intelligence can accelerate diagnostics and drug discovery — but only if the data it trains on stops excluding half the population.
body:
• Women's health receives only about 6% of private healthcare investment globally, with most capital historically concentrated in a narrow set of conditions like breast cancer and fertility.
  • AI is showing promise in closing diagnostic gaps — from detecting endometriosis years earlier to identifying coronary microvascular dysfunction that standard protocols miss in women — but models trained on male-skewed data risk amplifying existing biases.
  • Experts at the HLTH Europe 2026 conference outlined three AI deployment pillars: assisting clinical workflows, augmenting blind spots in female-specific pathology, and expanding specialist access to underserved regions.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly positioned as a tool to address one of healthcare's most stubborn structural problems: the chronic underfunding, under-researching and misdiagnosis of conditions that disproportionately affect women. But at a gathering of clinical leaders, investors and technologists at the HLTH Europe 2026 conference in Amsterdam, the consensus was clear — AI can only close the women's health gap if the data powering it improves dramatically.

The Scale of the Disparity

The numbers are stark. Women are twice as likely as men to experience anxiety disorders and comprise 80% of rheumatic disease patients. When a woman presents with a heart attack, she is twice as likely as a man to be misdiagnosed. Endometriosis, which is as prevalent as type 2 diabetes, carries an average diagnostic delay of 5 to 10 years, with surgery still the only definitive confirmation.

Yet women's health captures only about 6% of private healthcare investment, according to Helen Gaffney, principal of investments at Novo Holdings. The capital that does flow has clustered around a narrow band of well-understood conditions — breast cancer and fertility interventions — leaving vast therapeutic areas underfunded.

"If you're missing out on over 50% of patients because the data used to train a model is not catering to them, it's going to be a problem for your ROI and your patients."

— Petrina Kamya, PhD, global head of AI platforms, Insilico Medicine

Three Pillars of AI Deployment

Amira Romani, senior vice president at Siemens Healthineers, outlined a framework for deploying AI effectively across women's healthcare:

Assisting — driving workflow efficiency for routine clinical reads, freeing physicians to spend more time with patients. Ambient listening technology, which captures clinical summaries automatically, is already being integrated into workflows to reduce administrative burden while gathering longitudinal data.

Augmenting — overcoming historic blind spots. Male cardiac events typically present as macrovascular blockages detectable via standard chest pain protocols. Female cardiac pathology frequently manifests as coronary microvascular dysfunction in smaller vessels that human eyes routinely miss. AI can flag these subtle patterns for further evaluation.

Expanding — delivering specialist-level diagnostics to rural and underserved regions. In areas with severe physician shortages, AI-driven screening tools integrated into primary care clinics can provide expert-level capability where none existed before.

The Data Problem

The promise of AI in women's health runs directly into a data wall. Women have historically been underrepresented in clinical trials, meaning many diagnostic algorithms were trained on datasets skewed toward male populations. Without representative data, AI risks amplifying the very biases it aims to correct.

The U.S. National Science Foundation has begun addressing this through targeted initiatives, including a landmark workshop on using AI to better understand menopause. Drug discovery timelines have already been compressed from four-plus years to 13 months using machine learning, according to Insilico Medicine — but those gains depend entirely on training data quality.

Novel approaches are emerging. Existing mammography infrastructure is being repurposed: new algorithms scan for breast arterial calcification, a strong indicator of microvascular hardening that raises cardiovascular risk during perimenopause. "The technology is there, we just need to use it," said Romani.

Breaking the Investment Cycle

Early-stage investors cite insufficient late-stage capital to sustain companies, while late-stage funds point to a thin pipeline of mature innovations. A potential catalyst: two of the top 10 global pharmaceutical companies have recently entered the endometriosis pipeline, signaling market validation that could unlock early-stage funding.

The World Economic Forum has called for funders to require sex-disaggregated data in research, for researchers to treat sex as a first-order variable, and for regulators to create financial incentives and expedited approval pathways for treatments validated across both sexes. The question, as one WEF report framed it, is no longer whether AI can reshape healthcare — but whether data, incentives and standards can align quickly enough for the half of humanity that has been an afterthought.
